Tiny Towns: Napier

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Napier is a village with a history as unusual as its present day inhabitants.

Unique Selling Point:
Napier is a village with a history as unusual as its present day inhabitants. At the foot of the Soetmuisberg, it's located between Caledon and Bredasdorp and is about a two hour drive from Cape Town. Napier was founded in 1838 after a bitter dispute between two prominent neighbours, Michael van Breda and Pieter Voltelyn van der Byl, over where to build the community church. Van Breda wanted it built on his farm, while Van der Byl wanted the church on his property. The conflict was never resolved – instead, each man built his own church. The town of Bredasdorp grew around van Breda’s church, while Napier developed around van der Byl’s. The two men didn’t talk for ten years according to Napier residents. This story is told in the village, but is it fact or folklore?



Summary:
To this day, descendants of the van der Byl family still farm just outside of the town. One of the Van der Byl descendants, married a princess from Lichtenstein. Today, their son remains on the family farm, Fairfield, with his mother. He says if there ever was a dispute with the van Bredas, there isn't one now, and he is great friends with van Breda descendants. Napier has a population of about five thousand people.

The village itself is a blend of tradition and bohemian charm. The Dutch Reformed Church, built in the form of a Greek cross, houses a rare pipe organ made entirely from solid yellow copper.

Napier’s true charm lies in its people. About half the people who live there were born and raised there, including the local doctor. The rest are musicians, artists, and authors. Among them is Roger Lucey, a musician and former TV war journalist whose music was censored during Apartheid. His story is one of restistance, reinvention and quiet resilience, much like the town he now calls home.



Further information:
Mark Kerr owns local restaurant "Pascals" and has lived in the town for fifteen years. For him, its “a place with soul”… just far enough from Cape Town to avoid weekend crowds. His family visited nearby Arniston for holidays when he was a child, but Napier was always more than a pit stop en route, and now its his home. Betsie Wessels is another resident we meet - she has played the church's organ every week for the past fifty years. Napier is home to many interesting characters, and this feature will explore not just the town's history, but those who now inhabit it.

Script:


NATSOUND bells tolling

VO 1 In the village of Napier, every Sunday morning starts in the same way.

VO 2 With the sound of church bells ringing out across the valley - bell ropes pulled by hand, just as they were more than a century ago.

VO 3 Napier exists because of its church …or rather a dispute over where to build it.

VO 4 Whether fact or folklore, the story of two neighbours and their stubborn standoff is still told here.

LINK: You wouldn’t expect to find royalty at the end of a dirt road outside Napier. But, here on Fairfield farm heritage takes on a different shape. It’s a tale of old bloodlines rooted deep in South African soil.

VO 5 It’s here, that the van der Byls have lived for generations.

VO 6 Valerian van der Byl farms the land, as his forefathers did.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl / Napier Resident: This was obviously a very sparsely populated farming area back in the day. The basis to Napier being established was about the church.

VO 7 And critically where exactly to build it.

VO 8 The story goes that they couldn’t agree on the church’s location, so both men built their own church. Napier grew around this one, built in 1838 by Pieter Voltelyn van der Byl. The town of Bredasdorp, just 16kms away, grew around the other church.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl / Napier Resident: The van Bredas felt a need about naming a town after themselves. They started Bredadsdorp.

ERIN There’s clearly history here.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl: He’s a great friend of mine. He’s a great friend of mine, Mike. Anyway, so they named the town after themselves. We named the town Napier after the governor of the Cape and established the church. And that was basically the grounding that started Napier.

VO 9 Valerian is from a long line of van der Byls on his father’s side. They came to South Africa from the Netherlands in the 1600s. His mother married his father P.K van der Byl and she too has an interesting history.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl: She was born Princess of Lichtenstein. She moved to Rhodesia in 1979 and has accepted Africa as home and has been here ever since. You know, Mom has grown up like any normal person. There’s nothing different to her than the normal person on the streets. She might have a title, but that doesn’t change her.

VO 10 Valerian grew up in this house, clocks and doors salvaged from shipwrecks. The original building burnt down, but was rebuilt in 1853.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl: My father and a lot of my family all died in this house, but if there are ghosts, they’re good ghosts and they never bothered me.

VO 11 Valerian is very private and likes to keep a distance from the comparative bustle of the village - but he’s proud of what its’ become.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl :The town really took off in about 2001, 2002.. First restaurants opened, and suddenly village life came to it, where you had people from outside of the rural area moving in.

ERIN:Top of the recommended list for me to see.

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl: Well to see is our church is much bigger than the Bredasdorp church.

ERIN: You just couldn’t resist could you!

UPSOUND Valerian van der Byl: No, can’t resist that.

VO 12 The dutch reformed church dominates the tiny town of Napier which has only 5000 residents - but there are many things to see. From art galleries to antique shops.

LINK: Clip 589 / Card 2 At first glance Napier looks like any small sleepy town in South Africa, but spend a bit of time here and you’ll find that it’s home to the unexpected. And it’s anything but sleepy.

VO 13 It’s the colourful characters who live here now …who bring this town to life - like 71 year old Roger Lucey.

VO 14 Roger began his adult life as a musician, but he was silenced during Apartheid - his songs deemed a security risk.

UPSOUND Roger Lucey / Musician: I went from a very promising career to no career in a space of just a couple of years. It was quite devastating actually because I mean my first album which I recorded in 1979, was banned for possession and distribution.

VO 15 He became a broadcast journalist instead, covering conflict zones around the world.

UPSOUND Roger Lucey: It was never in my blood and, I aways, it scared me to be honest. I didn’t enjoy going out into the fray. It was a job and I had to do it. I went to Chechnya and Bosnia for some very dangerous situations and I ended up in a very poor state of mind at the end of all that.

VO 16 Eventually, after being awarded a scholarship, Roger enrolled for his masters degree at Duke University in America.

UPSOUND Roger Lucey (Clip 662/ Card 1) 07:15 I hadn’t finished high school, but I went and got a masters. And my poor old mother who had watched me go from one disaster to another during my life, just before she died I was able to tell her that you know I had straight As and “I think I’m alright now, mom”.

VO 17 Over ten years ago, he moved to Napier. A place where the unexpected happens.

UPSOUND Roger Lucey: I fell in love with a person who I had known for some time and, and she came and she bought a house here.

ERIN: So, what makes Napier so special?

UPSOUND Roger Lucey: The geography of the place is really lovely. It’s close to Cape Town, it’s close to the ocean. There are some lovely people. Like all towns you know, there’s also trouble and strife.

VO 18 It’s here that Roger began to sing again, sharpening his musical skills that had been dormant for so long.

UPSOUND Roger Lucey: For the first several years, I was very very quiet and under cover. I suppose I’ve introduced myself to the village through my songs and through my little shows.

NATSOUND: This is a song I wrote just before I came to live in Napier actually.

VO 19 And on a cold winter’s night we get to watch one of those shows at Pascals, the local restaurant.

VO 20 Living here, Roger’s put the ghosts of his past behind him.

VO 21 The town is surrounded by farms - one of them owned by Bruce Jack.

VO 22 His business Bruce Jack Wines is internationally recognised in the wine industry, but here in Napier is where he produces his very best wines.

UPSOUND Bruce Jack / Bruce Jack Wines Owner: When you take on farming, you take on a hell of a lot more than just the production of crops. You actually have to give yourself over to the land. This is a beautiful place to do that. This particular farm is the best place in the world to grow grapes.

VO 23 It’s cold here, but that’s good for the vineyards.

UPSOUND Bruce Jack: The big difference between this farm and other wine grape farms is the temperature, because of the altitude. And also because of our proximity to the oceans. It is the grimmest place in the Overberg to live if you don’t like the cold. I absolutely love it.

ERIN: Can we taste some of the fruits of your labour?
UPSOUND Bruce Jack: Yeah absolutely, so Immoveable Feast.

ERIN: Hemingway, Immoveable Feast.

UPSOUND Bruce Jack: Hemmingway, great name for a wine and this is our red blend from the farm. This is the pinnacle of what we produce on the farm.

ERIN: Cheers to that, and thank you so much.

UPSOUND Bruce Jack: Absolute pleasure. Thanks Erin, and thanks for visiting the tiny town of Napier.

ERIN: Ooh, that’s very nice.

VO 24 Despite the cool climate, Bruce wouldn’t live anywhere else. He loves the people, working the land, and the history of this special place.

VO 25 Just before leaving, we revisit the church at Napier’s centre.

VO 26 In 1974, Betsie Wessels made Napier her home - and she’s been playing the church organ ever since.

ERIN Subtitles: Tell me a bit about this organ. What makes it unique or special?

UPSOUND Betsie Wessels / Organist: Subtitles: It has a beautiful sound and the acoustics in the church are lovely, too. It’s complex – you really need to be quick on your feet and what you have to play. You have to stay sharp.

VO 27 She says the town’s changed a lot in the past fifty years.

UPSOUND Betsie Wessels: Subtitles: It used to be an Afrikaans-speaking community…Three quarters of our residents are English and the rest are Afrikaans. But there’s a good relationship between the people. You always greet everyone; that’s one of the nice things.

VO 28 People come from all over to concerts at the church to listen to the sounds of its unique organ.

UPSOUND Betsie Wessels: Subtitles: They love the organ. When there are concerts, people come from Bredasdorp, Struisbaai, Riviersonderend to listen. And if the church bell doesn’t ring in the town, people start complaining!

VO 29 At every weekly service, you’ll find Betsie, and the sounds of the organ as she plays it, ringing out.

The town of Bredasdorp grew around van Breda’s church, while Napier developed around van der Byl’s. The two men didn’t talk for ten years according to Napier residents. metadata.Summary: To this day, descendants of the van der Byl family still farm just outside of the town. One of the Van der Byl descendants, married a princess from Lichtenstein. Today, their son remains on the family farm, Fairfield, with his mother. He says if there ever was a dispute with the van Bredas, there isn't one now, and he is great friends with van Breda descendants. Napier has a population of about five thousand people. The village itself is a blend of tradition and bohemian charm. The Dutch Reformed Church, built in the form of a Greek cross, houses a rare pipe organ made entirely from solid yellow copper. Napier’s true charm lies in its people. About half the people who live there were born and raised there, including the local doctor. The rest are musicians, artists, and authors. Among them is Roger Lucey, a musician and former TV war journalist whose music was censored during Apartheid. His story is one of restistance, reinvention and quiet resilience, much like the town he now calls home.
metadata.Further information: Mark Kerr owns local restaurant "Pascals" and has lived in the town for fifteen years. For him, its “a place with soul”… just far enough from Cape Town to avoid weekend crowds. His family visited nearby Arniston for holidays when he was a child, but Napier was always more than a pit stop en route, and now its his home. Betsie Wessels is another resident we meet - she has played the church's organ every week for the past fifty years. Napier is home to many interesting characters, and this feature will explore not just the town's history, but those who now inhabit it.
